key.why: A load-use hazard: addi wants t0 in EX, but the load only has it at the end of MEM.

explanation:
## Line 2, the `addi` — a load-use hazard

This is the one hazard full forwarding cannot remove, and it is worth being able to draw.

Line the two instructions up by cycle:

```
cycle:        1    2    3    4    5    6
lw   t0       IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB
addi t1,t0         IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB
                             ^
                     addi needs t0 here, in cycle 4
```

`lw` computes the *address* in EX (cycle 3) and the loaded value only arrives at the end of **MEM**, in cycle 4. The `addi` wants that value at the start of its own EX, which is also cycle 4. The data is not there yet — it appears at the end of the cycle in which it is needed at the start.

So the pipeline inserts one bubble:

```
cycle:        1    2    3    4    5    6    7
lw   t0       IF   ID   EX   MEM  WB
addi t1,t0         IF   ID   **   EX   MEM  WB
                             ^^
                        one stall cycle
```

Now `addi` reaches EX in cycle 5, and MEM-to-EX forwarding hands the value over exactly in time.

## Why the other dependencies are free

Line 3, `sw t1, 0(a1)`, depends on `t1` from line 2 — and that is **not** a stall. `addi` produces `t1` at the end of its EX, and `sw` needs it one stage later than the load case did. EX-to-EX forwarding covers it with nothing to spare but nothing lost either.

That is the general rule, and it is the thing to take away:

| Producer | Result ready at end of | Forwarding to the next instruction's EX |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arithmetic (`add`, `addi`, `sll`) | EX | works, no stall |
| Load (`lw`, `lb`) | MEM | **one cycle too late — one stall** |

"Load-use hazard" is the name, and in a five-stage pipeline it costs exactly one cycle when the use is immediately after the load. If the use is two instructions later, there is no stall at all.

## The fix is free, and the compiler already does it

The listing has two independent copies of the same pattern. Interleave them:

```
lw   t0, 0(a0)
lw   t2, 8(a0)      # independent work, slotted into the gap
addi t1, t0, 4      # t0 has been ready since the end of the previous cycle
addi t3, t2, 4
sw   t1, 0(a1)
sw   t3, 8(a1)
```

Six instructions, same work, **no stalls**. The second `lw` fills the bubble, and by the time the first `addi` runs, `t0` has long since arrived.

This is *software pipelining*, and it is one of the oldest tricks in instruction scheduling. Any optimising compiler does it for you — which is part of why `-O0` code is so much slower than `-O2` code even when the algorithm is identical, and why hand-reading `-O2` output can be so disorienting: the instructions are deliberately not in source order.

## What a real CPU does instead

A modern out-of-order core does not stall here at all. It has a window of hundreds of instructions in flight and simply executes something else while the load completes, which is the same trick done in hardware at runtime rather than in the compiler at build time.

Which does *not* make the lesson obsolete, for two reasons. The in-order five-stage model is still how you reason about dependency chains, and dependency chains are what actually bound performance on an out-of-order machine once you are not memory-bound. And plenty of real silicon is still in-order — most microcontrollers, many embedded cores, and the GPU-adjacent parts of a system — where exactly this stall is visible in a cycle count.
